contributions: the TTC-awareness insight: an intermediate training checkpoint combined with an appropriately-chosen test-time-compute configuration can match or exceed a fully-trained checkpoint's accuracy at substantially fewer training FLOPs, demonstrated across multiple model families, sizes, and tasks

a TTC-aware early-stopping algorithm that fits a saturating accuracy-vs-training-FLOPs curve and a sigmoid accuracy-vs-K curve (queried at only small K values) to jointly decide when to stop training and what TTC sample budget to deploy with

a break-even bound identifying how much downstream inference volume can be served under TTC before its cost exceeds that of training a model fully without TTC, informing model-refresh cadence decisions

empirical validation of up to 92% training-FLOP reduction while maintaining or improving accuracy, across pretraining (TinyLlama, Pythia), continued training (FineMath) with multiple TTC aggregation methods, and a large-model fine-tuning setting (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct)
limitations: TTC-aware training's benefit is demonstrated primarily on smaller, publicly-available-intermediate-checkpoint model families (TinyLlama, Pythia, FineMath) because reproducing training for most large-scale frontier models with intermediate checkpoints would be prohibitively expensive; evaluation on a genuinely large frontier model uses only a single fine-tuning setting (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct, 1 epoch on GSM8K) rather than full pretraining. The TinyLlama-on-Math-500 experiment required additional targeted training to include sufficient math-domain data (since the originally fully-trained checkpoint scored 0%), and even then only a partial subset of intermediate checkpoints was usable due to compute constraints -- the paper states this as a practical limitation of fully exploiting the method across models and checkpoints, calling for more appropriate training resources/setup in future work. The break-even bound assumes a fixed ~6x ratio of training to inference FLOPs per token and a single serving-cost multiplier lambda, simplifications the paper does not further stress-test against real deployment cost variability.
method: Proposes TTC-aware training: during training, validation accuracy is collected from intermediate checkpoints and fit to an exponential saturation curve A_hat(B) = a(1-e^{-bB}) + c projecting expected final accuracy at a given training-FLOPs budget B, using only monotonically-non-decreasing validation points to filter training-induced fluctuation noise. A TTC-aware early-stopping algorithm (Algorithm 1) then, at each checkpoint, searches for the minimum sample count K* such that (i) the combined training-plus-TTC-inference FLOPs at that checkpoint stay below the full-budget-without-TTC cost, and (ii) the checkpoint's TTC-projected accuracy at K* meets or exceeds the projected final accuracy A_hat(B); training halts once this holds for a patience window of p consecutive checkpoints. To make per-checkpoint TTC evaluation practical without exhaustively sampling every K, a sigmoid curve A_hat_K(t) = L/(1+e^{-k(K-x0)}) is fit from a handful of small-K query points (K in {1,2,4}, which implicitly also yields results for all K'<=K), letting the optimal K* be extrapolated rather than searched exhaustively. A break-even bound is derived (assuming training FLOPs per token are ~6x inference FLOPs per token) giving the maximum downstream inference volume N_infer that can be served under TTC before the accumulated training-plus-serving cost exceeds that of a fully-trained baseline without TTC, expressed as a function of the training-FLOPs-savings ratio r and the relative TTC inference-cost multiplier lambda.
methods: Diverse Tree Search (DVTS, naive and weighted)
one_liner: TTC-aware training projects a model's expected validation accuracy under test-time compute (via an exponential-saturation curve fit to intermediate checkpoints) to identify an early-stopping point where an intermediate checkpoint plus TTC inference matches or exceeds a fully-trained checkpoint's accuracy at a fraction of training FLOPs -- up to 92% training-FLOP savings while preserving or improving accuracy, validated across TinyLlama, Pythia, FineMath, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct.
problem: Prior work shows test-time compute (TTC) -- iterative sampling, verifier-guided search -- lets smaller models rival or surpass larger ones at lower total cost, but existing training studies compare only fully-trained models of different sizes, overlooking how performance evolves with training FLOPs within a single model; existing early-stopping methods remain TTC-agnostic (they optimize only single-inference validation accuracy) and existing TTC techniques (especially repeated sampling) do not predict an efficient number of samples K, so training and inference compute are optimized separately rather than jointly.

relevance.overthinking: Only indirectly relevant: this paper is about training-time compute efficiency (how much pretraining/fine-tuning FLOPs are needed before a checkpoint plus a fixed test-time-compute budget matches a fully-trained model), not about single-response reasoning-trace length or the inference-time overthinking behavior this archive centrally tracks. Its shared vocabulary (test-time compute, Pass@K, early stopping) reflects the same broader test-time-scaling literature this archive draws on, but the object being optimized (a training schedule, not a reasoning trace) is a different question.

results: Across TinyLlama (HumanEval, DROP), Pythia (1B/2.8B/6.9B, HumanEval, GSM8K), and a continued-training FineMath setup (10B/30B/40B/50B tokens, Math-500), the TTC-aware effect is consistent: an intermediate checkpoint using TTC (e.g. Pass@8) matches or exceeds a fully-trained baseline's accuracy without TTC, at substantially fewer training FLOPs -- e.g. TinyLlama/HumanEval: an intermediate checkpoint achieves a +0.45 percentage-point accuracy gain over the final checkpoint at 92.44% training-FLOP savings (85.5% net savings after accounting for the extra TTC-inference FLOPs consumed during training itself); Pythia-2.8B at 80k training steps with Pass@8 (8.84% HumanEval) not only matches but surpasses its own 143k-step baseline (6.7%) and even the much larger 6.9B baseline at 143k steps (6.8%). A recurring cross-model-size pattern: when an intermediate checkpoint uses a larger K than the fully-trained baseline (e.g. Pass@8 vs. the baseline's Pass@4), it can often match or surpass the baseline's accuracy while still saving FLOPs; comparing checkpoints at the *same* K, the fully-trained baseline always wins, but only at the cost of substantially more FLOPs. In the FineMath continued-training setting, even a lower-budget checkpoint at a larger K frequently surpasses a higher-budget checkpoint evaluated at smaller K (e.g. at K=4, the 10B-token checkpoint's 24.73% exceeds the 50B-token checkpoint's K=2 result of 18.28%), a pattern that recurs across multiple budget pairs and holds across simple Pass@K, majority voting, Diverse Tree Search (naive and weighted), and Compute-Optimal Search aggregation methods, not just raw Pass@K -- DVTS-Weighted consistently gives the best overall TTC performance and Compute-Optimal Search an approximate upper bound. The insight extends to a large-model fine-tuning scenario (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct on GSM8K, 1 epoch): Pass@K over intermediate checkpoints is non-monotonic, and TTC-aware selection identifies an intermediate checkpoint with Pass@2 outperforming the final checkpoint by more than 10 percentage points. The full early-stopping algorithm (with monotonic-fluctuation filtering) substantially outperforms naive PyTorch-style early stopping: on TinyLlama-HumanEval, the naive baseline either halts too early (large FLOPs savings but a meaningful accuracy drop) or barely saves compute at all depending on patience, while the proposed method achieves up to 92% FLOPs savings while *improving* accuracy by 0.44%; ablating the fluctuation-filtering step shows it specifically matters -- with filtering, HumanEval/DROP FLOPs savings reach 90.7%/87.0% at +0.6%/+1.0% accuracy gain, versus 56.8%/72.7% savings at +2.05%/+2.08% gain without it (filtering trades a smaller accuracy margin for substantially larger compute savings by avoiding stopping at a noisy local peak). Patience-sensitivity analysis shows a mid-range patience value (~10) gives the best trade-off; patience 0 stops too early (large negative accuracy delta), while very high patience approaches the full-training baseline with diminishing FLOPs savings. The derived break-even bound, applied illustratively at r~0.2 (80% training savings) and lambda~1.2 (20% relative TTC-serving overhead), implies TTC-aware training and deployment remains cost-favorable for up to ~70B downstream inference samples before the model needs to be refreshed via further training.
